t: 21 Things You Should Never Do To Students
q: Effective classroom management is as much about what you don’t do. As it is about what you do .
The removal of common but ultimately hurtful strategies . . . Can have a profound impact on behavior.
In that spirit, and truth, what follows are 21 things you should never do to students. Ever, ever, ever.
The whys and hows of all 21—except #16, which we’ll cover in a future article—have been written about extensively on this website.
In the meantime, although many of the “never dos” listed above are common teaching practice, make no mistake. They’re bad for students and bad for your classroom.
Removing them from your classroom management toolkit will put you far ahead of the curve. It will make you more effective and more influential and bring a natural calm to your class.

t: Why The Ordinary, Everyday, And Mundane Is Key To Good Behavior And Academic Improvement
q: It’s only natural to want to focus on what matters. To concern yourself primarily with content, lessons, and academic performance.
The truth is, everything you do as a class affects how well your students behave and progress.

In fact, it’s the wee little boring details—like the way students turn in work or transition to a new activity or take out their laptops—that have the greatest impact on behavior, success habits, and the like.

Success is in the details” is as much or more true for teaching as any other profession. Yet, it’s the most underutilized and underappreciated key to effective classroom management and academic improvement.
Visitors to my own classroom are often surprised at my students’ sense of freedom and casualness. In fact, we often walk across campus not in a line, but in one silent but happy herd.
It’s the focus on what most teachers gloss over that is the secret to inspiring pride, boosting morale, improving behavior . . .

t: How Not To Feel Resentment Over Difficult Students
q: It’s normal to feel angry. How could you not? You have a student who is ruining your school year.
If you’re a regular reader of SCM, however, then you know that resentment does you no good. In fact, it makes things worse because it’s something you can’t hide, no matter how hard you try.
The solution is to realize that it’s not the student’s fault. Somewhere along the line they’ve been let down by the adults in their life.
That’s not to say that they’re not responsible for their own behavior. They are, 100%. But you’re the one standing in front of them.
Grasping this reality has a way of putting things into perspective and replacing the resentment you can’t seem to shake with compassion and understanding.
This doesn’t mean that you’ll ever lower your standards or fail to hold them accountable. Love, after all, is not an emotion. Rather, it’s the active pursuit of what’s best for another.
